newsitem.title: USA: U.S West Coast crude rises with NYMEX, trade quiet.
newsitem.headline: U.S West Coast crude rises with NYMEX, trade quiet.

text.p: U.S. West Coast crude oil prices rose Tuesday with other domestic oil markets while local traders awaited key supply reports, oil companies said.

Spot crude oil trade remained flat ahead of the American Petroleum Institute's weekly inventory report, due out late Tuesday. Traders also waited the results of a local auction of California Central Valley grades, traders said.
West Coast (PADD 5) crude oil inventories fell 3.7 million barrels as of June 27, according to API reports, but traders saw no impact on the market.
Separatelyh, the U.S Department of Energy (DOE) held a bi-monthly auction Tuesday of lighter crudes from its Elk Hills Naval Petroleum Reserve in Bakersfield, Calif.
The crudes, which are shipped down Line 63, from the Central California oil fields to Los Angeles refineries, sell at discount to a formula price.
Celeron Trading and Transportation won the most Elk Hills oil, taking 7,500 barrels-per-day at a price of $2.186 under a West Texas Intermediate price formula, traders said.
Line 63 pipeline has ample space to carry crude this month, the line's owner, ARCO, said.
Meanwhile, outright prices for Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude oil, moved with other U.S. grades.

West Texas Intermediate (WTI) August cash crude prices rose 23 cents a barrel, while the NYMEX futures price climbed 32 cents, amid a flurry of buying on concerns of delayed Iraq crude exports and a report of falling domestic inventories.
The discount for Alaskan North Slope (ANS) crude, the regional benchmark, remained unchanged at $2.16 under August West Texas Intermediate/Cushing (WTI) crude.
Line 63 barrels also rose with NYMEX and cash WTI crude markets.
Kern River and Wilmington crudes -- California heavy grades -- edged up after a major oil company raised posted prices Monday and Tuesday.
